anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: How is the abdomen divided into nine regions?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: By two vertical (midclavicular) planes and two horizontal planes (the subcostal & transtubercular).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the nine abdominal regions.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Top: right hypochondrium, epigastrium, left hypochondrium; middle: right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar; bottom: right iliac, hypogastrium, left iliac.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What structures lie in the transpyloric plane (L1)?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The pylorus, fundus of the gallbladder, neck of the pancreas, origin of the SMA, and the hila of the kidneys — midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Where is McBurney's point, and what does it overlie?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: One-third of the way from the ASIS to the umbilicus — the surface marking of the base of the appendix.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the two layers of superficial fascia below the umbilicus.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Camper’s fascia (fatty, superficial) and Scarpa’s fascia (membranous, deep).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the layers of the anterior abdominal wall from superficial to deep.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Skin → Camper’s & Scarpa’s fascia → muscles → transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal fat → parietal peritoneum.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is Scarpa's fascia continuous with, and why does it matter?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: With Colles’ fascia in the perineum and the dartos of the scrotum/penis — explaining how extravasated urine tracks into the scrotum & abdominal wall.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Give the fibre directions of the three flat abdominal muscles.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: External oblique — inferomedial (“hands in pockets”); internal oblique — superomedial; transversus abdominis — transverse.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is the linea alba, and the linea semilunaris?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The linea alba is the midline fusion of the aponeuroses; the linea semilunaris is the curved lateral border of rectus abdominis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is the innervation of the anterior abdominal wall muscles?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The anterior rami of T7–T12 (& L1) — the thoraco-abdominal (and subcostal/iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal) nerves.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Describe the rectus sheath ABOVE the arcuate line.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The internal oblique aponeurosis splits: anterior wall = EO + anterior IO lamina; posterior wall = posterior IO lamina + transversus abdominis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Describe the rectus sheath BELOW the arcuate line.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: All three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis, so the posterior wall is only transversalis fascia (a weak point).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Where is the arcuate line?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: About one-third of the way from the umbilicus to the pubic symphysis — the lower limit of the posterior rectus sheath aponeurosis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is the inguinal ligament and its attachments?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Where are the deep and superficial inguinal rings?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The deep ring is a defect in the transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; the superficial ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What forms the walls of the inguinal canal?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Anterior: EO aponeurosis (+ IO laterally); posterior: transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon medially); roof: arching IO & TA fibres; floor: inguinal ligament (+ lacunar ligament).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What are the contents of the inguinal canal?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The spermatic cord (♂) or round ligament of the uterus (♀), plus the ilioinguinal nerve (which lies on the cord, not within it).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the three arteries of the spermatic cord.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The testicular artery, the cremasteric artery, and the artery to the vas (ductus) deferens.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the nerves associated with the spermatic cord.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (which is itself the nerve to cremaster) and sympathetic (autonomic) fibres; the ilioinguinal nerve runs on the cord (not within its coverings) — together these make up the traditional “three nerves.”

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: List the three 'other' contents of the spermatic cord.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The vas (ductus) deferens, the pampiniform plexus of veins, and lymphatics.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the three coverings of the spermatic cord and their origins.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: External spermatic fascia (from external oblique), cremasteric fascia (from internal oblique), internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What are the boundaries of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Medial — lateral border of rectus abdominis; lateral — inferior epigastric vessels; inferior — inguinal ligament.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Distinguish an indirect from a direct inguinal hernia.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Indirect — through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; congenital (patent processus vaginalis); may reach the scrotum. Direct — through Hesselbach’s triangle, medial to the vessels; acquired (weak wall).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: How do you clinically distinguish an inguinal from a femoral hernia?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: A hernia above & medial to the pubic tubercle is inguinal; one below & lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: How can pressure over the deep ring differentiate hernia types?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: After reduction, pressure over the deep ring (just above the mid-inguinal point / femoral pulse) controls an indirect hernia; a direct hernia still bulges.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Psoas major, quadratus lumborum, iliacus (and transversus abdominis laterally).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is iliopsoas, and its main action?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Psoas major + iliacus, inserting on the lesser trochanter — the chief flexor of the hip.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: Name the three folds on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: The median umbilical fold (urachus), the medial umbilical folds (obliterated umbilical arteries), and the lateral umbilical folds (inferior epigastric vessels).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What is a rectus sheath haematoma?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: Bleeding from torn inferior epigastric vessels (typically below the arcuate line) → a painful abdominal wall mass that can mimic an acute abdomen.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.front: What dermatome is the umbilicus, and its clinical relevance?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.back: T10 — early appendicitis pain is referred here (peri-umbilical) before localising to the right iliac fossa.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The transpyloric plane lies at which vertebral level?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The transpyloric plane of Addison lies at L1, midway between the xiphisternum and umbilicus, crossing the pylorus, pancreatic neck, SMA origin and renal hila.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The two layers of superficial fascia below the umbilicus are:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Below the umbilicus the superficial fascia splits into Camper's (fatty, superficial) and Scarpa's (membranous, deep).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The fibres of the external oblique muscle run:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: External oblique fibres pass inferomedially ('hands in pockets'); internal oblique runs at right angles (superomedial) and transversus abdominis is horizontal.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Below the arcuate line, the posterior wall of the rectus sheath is formed by:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus abdominis, leaving only transversalis fascia posteriorly — a relative weak point.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The deep inguinal ring lies in the transversalis fascia, in what relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; an indirect hernia therefore enters lateral to these vessels.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The inguinal ligament runs between which two bony points?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The inguinal ligament is the rolled lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: An indirect inguinal hernia passes through the deep ring, which is located:
options: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels (congenital, via a patent processus vaginalis); a direct hernia is medial (Hesselbach's triangle).

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through:
options: Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
The superficial ring only, lateral to the vessels
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: A direct hernia pushes through the weakened posterior wall in Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Which is the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded medially by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: A hernia located BELOW and LATERAL to the pubic tubercle is most likely a:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: A hernia below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is femoral; an inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the tubercle.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Which of the following is a covering of the spermatic cord derived from internal oblique?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The cremasteric fascia (and cremaster muscle) derive from internal oblique; the external spermatic fascia is from external oblique and the internal spermatic fascia from transversalis fascia.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Which structure lies ON the spermatic cord rather than within it?
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve pierces internal oblique to enter the canal, lies on the cord (not within its coverings), and exits through the superficial ring.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The anterior abdominal wall muscles are innervated by the anterior rami of:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The thoraco-abdominal nerves (T7–T11), the subcostal (T12) and iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal (L1) supply the anterior abdominal wall.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The median umbilical fold contains the remnant of the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The median umbilical fold overlies the urachus (median umbilical ligament); the medial folds contain the obliterated umbilical arteries and the lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: McBurney's point, overlying the appendix base, is located:
options: Halfway between the ASIS and pubic tubercle
One-third from the ASIS to the umbilicus
One-third from the umbilicus to the ASIS
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: McBurney's point is one-third of the way along a line from the ASIS to the umbilicus.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: A rectus sheath haematoma typically results from injury to the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Tearing of the inferior epigastric vessels (especially below the arcuate line, where they are unsupported posteriorly) produces a rectus sheath haematoma that can mimic an acute abdomen.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Dilated para-umbilical veins ('caput medusae') indicate:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Caput medusae results from portosystemic anastomosis at the umbilicus in portal hypertension, via recanalised para-umbilical veins.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: The chief flexor of the hip, formed by psoas major and iliacus, is the:
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: Psoas major and iliacus unite as iliopsoas, inserting on the lesser trochanter — the principal hip flexor; a psoas abscess can track to the groin.

anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.question: Early appendicitis produces peri-umbilical pain because the umbilicus is the ____ dermatome.
anatomy__ABDOMEN__Abdominal Wall & Osteo.explanation: The umbilicus is the T10 dermatome; early visceral appendiceal pain is referred here before localising to the right iliac fossa.
